title: Newton’s Views on Space, Time, and Motion

summaries.example: Imagine two children sitting in a bus. To one another, they seem still. To someone standing on the sidewalk, they move along the road. Newton would say that this is a relative motion: it depends on what we compare the children with. He also thought there was a deeper kind of motion, called true or absolute motion, connected with movement through absolute space.
summaries.summary: Newton argued that space, time, and motion are not only names for relationships between objects. He thought space exists independently of bodies and that time passes evenly, even when things speed up, slow down, or stop changing. He called these absolute space and absolute time. The spaces and times we use in daily life are relative measures, based on objects, clocks, or cycles. Newton also said that true motion is movement through absolute space. Earlier thinkers, including Aristotle and Descartes, offered different pictures. Aristotle rejected empty space and treated time as a measure of change. Atomists allowed empty space. Descartes identified space with matter, so he also rejected a vacuum. Newton’s bucket example showed that water can have effects of rotation even when it is not moving compared with the bucket. This supported his claim that nearby objects alone do not fully explain motion.
key_ideas: Newton separated space and time themselves from the ways people measure them.
He thought true motion was more than simply moving compared with nearby objects.
Some earlier thinkers denied that empty space could exist.
The rotating-bucket example was meant to connect motion with its effects, not simply to show that absolute motion can be seen directly.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas shaped classical physics for centuries. They also show that science can depend on philosophical questions: What kinds of things exist? Is empty space real? Is time independent of events? Newton’s view later faced criticism from thinkers such as Leibniz, Berkeley, and Mach, and modern relativity changed how space and time are described. Studying the debate helps us understand why measuring motion is not always the same as explaining what motion really is.

important_terms.definition: The idea that space exists on its own, even if no physical objects are in a particular place.
The idea that time keeps passing at the same steady rate, whether or not events are happening.
A motion described by comparing one object with another object, such as a bus moving compared with the road.
A completely empty region with no bodies or matter in it.

questions_to_think_about: If you are sitting on a moving bus, are you moving or still? What are you comparing yourself with?
Could there be a place with no objects in it at all?
Why might a clock or the movement of the Sun be only a way to measure time, rather than time itself?

summaries.example: Consider a bucket hanging from a twisted cord. At first, the bucket spins quickly while the water is nearly still relative to the room; the water’s surface remains fairly flat. Later, the water spins with the bucket, so the water and bucket are at relative rest, yet the water rises along the sides. Newton used this contrast to argue that the water’s rotational state cannot be defined solely by its motion relative to the bucket. The experiment was part of a larger argument that an adequate account of true motion requires reference to absolute space.
summaries.summary: The entry examines Newton’s metaphysical and physical account of space, time, and motion. In the Scholium to the Principia, Newton distinguishes absolute time, which passes uniformly without dependence on external changes, from relative time, which is measured through clocks and cycles. He similarly distinguishes absolute space, an immovable framework independent of bodies, from relative spaces defined by reference to bodies. Absolute motion is change of absolute place; relative motion is change of place within a chosen system of bodies. The entry stresses a subtle point about Newton’s arguments. His opponents generally did not deny that a body has a true state of motion or rest. Rather, they sought to analyze that state using relations among bodies or their causes. Newton’s arguments from properties, causes, and effects aim to show that such analyses are inadequate without absolute places. The rotating bucket shows that rotational effects do not track motion relative to the bucket: the water can be relatively moving without the characteristic effect, and later can be relatively still while the effect is strongest. The entry also explains the historical alternatives. Aristotle defended a finite material plenum and treated time as a measure of change. Atomists accepted an infinite void. Descartes identified body with extension and therefore denied that empty space was possible. Newton’s framework shaped classical physics until relativity introduced new structures and reopened the philosophical issues.
key_ideas: Newton distinguished absolute quantities from relative, apparent, and commonly measured quantities.

The entry emphasizes that Newton’s main target was not the claim that true motion exists; many opponents accepted that each body is truly moving or at rest. His target was the analysis of true motion.
Newton argued that local relations, impressed forces, and rotational effects cannot by themselves define true motion without reference to absolute space.

The bucket experiment and the revolving-globes example serve different purposes: the bucket supports the analysis of true motion, while the globes illustrate how absolute motion might be inferred indirectly.
Aristotle’s plenum, atomist theories of the void, and Descartes’ identification of body with extension formed important background to Newton’s position.
Newton’s views dominated classical physics, but later debates over relativity challenged and transformed the framework.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate links abstract metaphysics with concrete scientific practice. Questions about whether space and time exist independently influenced how philosophers interpreted motion, force, astronomy, and the possibility of a vacuum. The entry also corrects a common reading of the bucket experiment: Newton was not simply trying to prove that absolute motion can be directly observed. He was arguing that the concept of true motion cannot be reduced to selected relative motions. At the same time, he acknowledged that absolute space is not directly sensed and that true motion must be inferred through apparent differences, causes, and effects. important_terms.definition: Newton’s proposed real, immovable spatial framework, existing independently of bodies and providing the places through which bodies truly move.
Newton’s proposed duration that flows uniformly and independently of particular changes, clocks, or physical processes.
A theory that treats space and time as real entities with their own mode of existence, rather than merely as relations among bodies.
A theory that analyzes space, time, or motion in terms of relations among bodies or events, rather than independently existing spatial or temporal entities.
Motion through absolute space; in Newton’s framework, the translation of a body from one absolute place to another.
A space with no body or matter in it. Atomists accepted its possibility, while Aristotle and Descartes rejected it for different reasons.
The tendency associated with rotation for a body or its parts to move away from the axis of rotation; Newton treated it as an effect related to true circular motion.
A scholium is an explanatory or supplementary discussion. Newton’s Scholium in the Principia distinguishes absolute and relative time, space, place, and motion.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the water’s behavior in the bucket create a problem for defining rotation only by comparing the water with the bucket?
Can a physical effect provide evidence for a theory about what space is, or only for a theory about how bodies behave?
Why does the principle of Galilean relativity make uniform straight-line motion difficult to distinguish experimentally from rest?
How does Descartes’ identification of body with extension rule out a vacuum?
Does later relativity simply refute Newton, or does it change the background assumptions of the older debate?

summaries.example: Think about a skateboard rolling down a sidewalk. A friend standing on the sidewalk says the skateboard is moving. A person sitting on the skateboard may say that a backpack beside them is not moving. Both descriptions are relative: they depend on the chosen comparison point. Newton agreed that such descriptions are useful, but he argued that they do not tell the whole story. He believed there is also true motion, which is motion through absolute space.
summaries.summary: This entry explains Newton’s account of space, time, and motion and the earlier ideas he was responding to. Newton held that absolute space exists independently of bodies and remains immovable. Absolute time passes uniformly, whether physical events are fast, slow, or absent. By contrast, relative space and relative time are practical measures based on bodies, clocks, astronomical cycles, or other changes. Newton defined true motion as movement through absolute space. This does not mean that he thought ordinary observations were useless; rather, apparent motions are comparisons between bodies and may not reveal the complete motion of either one. Earlier theories disagreed about the foundations. Aristotle described the universe as a material plenum, with no empty space, and treated time as a measure of motion or change. Atomists believed matter consists of tiny parts separated by void. Descartes rejected a vacuum because he identified body with extension: an empty extended region would then be impossible. Newton’s Scholium argues that true motion cannot be defined using only local relationships. The rotating bucket helps make this point. When water is moving relative to the bucket, its surface may remain flat; later, when water and bucket move together relative to the room, the water rises at the sides. Newton took this difference to show that rotational effects are not determined simply by motion relative to surrounding bodies. The entry also explains that the final example of two connected revolving globes has a different role: it concerns how true motion might be inferred indirectly from effects such as tension.
key_ideas: Newton’s Scholium separates absolute space, time, place, and motion from their relative and ordinary measurements.
Aristotle treated time as a measure of change and denied empty space; atomists defended the void; Descartes identified space with matter.
Newton’s opponents often accepted that true motion exists, but tried to explain it through relations among bodies or through causes.
The rotating bucket example is used to challenge definitions of true rotation based only on motion relative to nearby objects.
Newton’s theory connected philosophical claims about space and time with the scientific structure of classical mechanics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Newton’s position influenced physics from the seventeenth century until the development of relativity. It also illustrates how scientific theories can contain philosophical commitments about what exists. The debate is not only about choosing a convenient reference point. It asks whether there is a real spatial and temporal framework behind our measurements, and whether motion can be fully explained by relationships among objects. Later critics, including Leibniz, Berkeley, and Mach, questioned Newton’s conclusions, while relativity changed the accepted account of space and time. important_terms.definition: Space that Newton believed exists independently of physical bodies and does not move or change its arrangement.
Time understood as passing evenly on its own, not merely as a count of changes in the world.
Motion described by comparing an object with another object or reference system.
The claim that space and time are real entities, rather than only relationships among bodies and events.
The view that space, time, and motion can be explained through relationships among bodies or events.
An entirely empty region. Ancient atomists accepted the possibility of a void; Aristotle and Descartes rejected it.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people give different descriptions of the same motion without one of them being wrong?
Why might Newton think a clock measures time without being identical to time itself?
What problem does a vacuum create for a theory saying that space is nothing more than matter arranged in different ways?
Why is the water’s rising up the bucket’s sides important if the water and bucket eventually rotate together?
What would count as evidence for something that cannot be directly seen?
